new_statements.rule_in_words: Gangou is a (reduced) tone language: three lexical tones /11, 35, 55/ contrast on the first syllable of di-/polysyllables, only two (high vs low-rising) on isolation monosyllables; non-initial syllables show extensive tone neutralization and there are 'reduced/destressed' monomoraic syllables (SM-neutral-tone type word-finally, plus reduced i/u syllables in any position). The source gives NO rule for where word stress falls; it explicitly flags stress as an open question that 'may play an important role'. Kerbs 2021 (Himalayan Linguistics 20(3): 12, 23-24) restates the 2-3-tone analysis and never mentions stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Toneless enclitics (e.g. perfect -lio) take their pitch from the preceding syllable; possible Hui vs non-Hui differences untested; author unsure whether low vs rising contrast is phonemic.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone analysis restricted to monosyllables (isolation/utterance-final) and disyllabic words; the full tonal contrast is word-initial, suggesting a left-headed tonal domain (Kerbs 2021: 24 compares Shanghai), but this is not framed as stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Kerbs's data: three speakers (one Tu/Monguor woman, two Han men) from Gangou Township, Minhe County, recorded 2017 in Gangou and Xining; Hui speakers' Gangou not sampled and may differ. Same variety as Glottolog gang1272 'Gangou' (no ISO code); locally part of the Ledu–Minhe group of Qinghai (Zhongyuan/Northwest) Mandarin, heavily restructured under Mangghuer (Minhe Monguor) contact.

sources.locator: ch. 5 Conclusions, p. 67 (with sec. 4.2 p. 54 and sec. 4.1 p. 53)
sources.note: Only dedicated phonology of Gangou. Ch. 4 'Suprasegmental phonology' (pp. 53-66): Gangou is tonal -- three underlying tones (11, 35, 55), reduced to two in monosyllables, extensive tone neutralization in non-initial syllables; 4.1 describes 'reduced (destressed, monomoraic) syllables', more frequent than Standard Mandarin neutral tone and not confined to word-final position. No rule for word-stress placement; p. 67 explicitly: 'Stress (and possible ensuing tonal reduction) may play an important role in the prosodic system of Gangou' -- i.e. stress left uninvestigated.
